title: Is Christianity Good for Women?
excerpt: Christians have often been bad for women and have used the Bible to do it, Jesus was not, and the record of his church runs both ways for reasons the church has to tell on itself.
body:
A woman sits in the back row of a church she has attended for eleven years. Last spring she told a leader what was happening in her house, and he opened a Bible to a verse about wives. A few rows up, a girl of fourteen is working out why every voice she has ever heard from the front belongs to a man, and what that says about her. Across town a graduate student who left the faith keeps a list of the verses that drove her out, and nobody in her old congregation has ever asked to see it. And somewhere a grandmother who cleaned offices for forty years will tell anyone who asks that church was the first place in her life where she was called by her name and asked what she thought.

All four are telling the truth about what they have seen, and any answer to the question in the title has to be one all four could sit through. The charge against Christianity is stronger than most Christians have let themselves hear, so it comes first here, with nothing softened.

One thing comes before the argument. If you are being hurt, by a husband, in a church or anywhere else, it is not what God asks you to bear. Tell someone you trust today; the Find Help page (/help) lists places to turn.

## The Charge

It was put most sharply by Elizabeth Cady Stanton in 1895, in the introduction to *The Woman's Bible*. When the women of her century asked for a different place in society and in the church, she wrote, "they were referred to the Bible for an answer." She summed up what they were shown there: "The Bible teaches that woman brought sin and death into the world, that she precipitated the fall of the race, that she was arraigned before the judgment seat of Heaven, tried, condemned and sentenced."

The texts are not hard to find. One of the Ten Commandments lists a neighbor's wife alongside his house, his servants and his ox as things not to be coveted (Exodus 20:17). A law in Deuteronomy says that a man who "seizes" an unbetrothed virgin "and lies with her" must pay her father fifty shekels of silver, "and she shall be his wife, because he has violated her" (Deuteronomy 22:28–29). In the New Testament the lines are better known. "Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord" (Ephesians 5:22). "The women should keep silent in the churches" (1 Corinthians 14:34). "I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet. For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor" (1 Timothy 2:12–14).

Then there is what the church's teachers made of those lines. Tertullian, writing in North Africa around the year 200, told Christian women, "You are the devil's gateway." John Chrysostom, the great preacher of the fourth century, taught from the verse about Eve that women are more easily deceived than men, and that reading held for much of the church's history. In the thirteenth century Thomas Aquinas, following Aristotle, wrote that "as regards the individual nature, woman is defective and misbegotten." He added that in the wider purpose of nature, which depends on God, she is no mistake. The first half of the sentence still says what it says.

At full strength the charge is that these men weren't misreading their Bible. A faith with those verses in it will go on producing those teachers, the argument runs, and women will go on paying. The woman in the back row is the evidence.

## What Has to Be Granted

Most of the history has to be granted. The quotations are real and they are a small sample. For centuries women who asked for more were told that Scripture had closed the question, and Stanton was reporting what had been said to her.

The worst part has to be granted too. The words about submission have been used on women in danger. A wife who said she was being beaten has been sent home with Ephesians 5. A woman who reported what a church leader did to her has been asked to think of his ministry. The site's page on [abuse and cover-up](/questions/morality/abuse-and-cover-up) says that church leaders knew of abuse and protected their institutions, and it says no argument excuses that. None is offered here.

The hard verses are also really there. Christians who say the Bible has only ever lifted women up haven't read Stanton, and they haven't listened to the women in their own pews. Some of the Old Testament laws assume a world in which a daughter's future was her father's to arrange and a wife's standing depended on her husband. The law in Deuteronomy made the man responsible for the woman for the rest of his life and forbade him to divorce her, in a society where she might otherwise have been left with nothing, and a related law in Exodus let her father refuse the marriage. That explains what the law was for. It doesn't make it a law any reader today would write, and the site's own notes call it difficult.

## The World These Words Entered

A letter survives from a working man named Hilarion, working away from home in Alexandria, to a woman named Alis who was expecting a child. It is dated 1 BC. He tells her not to worry, asks how he could ever forget her, and gives one instruction. In one English translation it reads: "if you bear a child and it is male, let it be; if it is female, cast it out."

Hilarion was an ordinary man making an ordinary family decision. A newborn could be left outside to die or to be picked up by a stranger, and Hilarion's letter says which child he meant to keep. The faith entered that world, and its critics noticed at once who was drawn to it. Celsus, a pagan critic of the second century, sneered that Christians were able to win over only "the silly, and the mean, and the stupid, with women and children." Origen, who copied the words out in order to answer them, replied that the gospel does invite such people, and others as well.

## What Jesus Did

Christians measure the church by Jesus, and so should its critics. He was a Jewish teacher, and Israel's Scriptures already had Deborah judging the nation and Huldah speaking for God to a king's officials. He was not rescuing women from Judaism. What the Gospels record is how he dealt with the women in front of him, and the pattern doesn't break.

He taught them as disciples. Mary of Bethany "sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching" (Luke 10:39), which was how a student sat before a teacher. When her sister wanted her back in the kitchen, Jesus answered, "Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her" (Luke 10:42). Women traveled with him and paid for the work: Luke names Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna, "and many others, who provided for them out of their means" (Luke 8:3). At a well in Samaria his own disciples came back and "marveled that he was talking with a woman" (John 4:27). He called a woman bent double for eighteen years "a daughter of Abraham" (Luke 13:16), and he said it in a synagogue, in front of the men who had objected to her healing.

When he spoke about lust, he laid the weight on the man: "everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart" (Matthew 5:28). Nothing in the sentence blames what she wore. When a woman poured ointment on his head and the men at the table called it waste, he said that "wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her" (Mark 14:9).

At the end, most of the men were gone. "There were also women looking on from a distance" (Mark 15:40), the same women who had followed him from Galilee. All four Gospels say women found the tomb empty, in a world where a woman's word counted for little as testimony. Luke doesn't hide how the apostles took the news: "these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them" (Luke 24:11).

## What the First Churches Did

At Pentecost Peter explained what was happening with a line from the prophet Joel about sons and daughters prophesying. Paul, the author of the hardest sentences in the charge, closed his greatest letter with a list of names, and the site's Study Bible note counts at least ten women among them. Phoebe is "a servant of the church at Cenchreae" and "a patron of many and of myself as well" (Romans 16:1–2); the word for servant is the one used elsewhere for the office of deacon. Prisca is a fellow worker, named before her husband. Mary "has worked hard for you" (Romans 16:6). Junia is named with honor in a phrase whose exact sense is still argued.

To husbands he gave the longer command and the heavier one: "love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her" (Ephesians 5:25). On the marriage bed he said the same of both, and in his world the second half of the sentence was the strange half: "the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does" (1 Corinthians 7:4). And he wrote the line that has stood over the whole argument since: "there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28).

The churches acted on it in ways their neighbors could see. The earliest Christian manual outside the New Testament, the *Didache*, told converts, "thou shalt not murder a child by abortion nor kill that which is begotten." Justin, writing to the emperor in the 150s, said Christians "have been taught that to expose newly-born children is the part of wicked men." The site's history course says it in one sentence: they took in the infants Rome left exposed. A daughter like the one Hilarion wrote about was among the children they would not leave.

Widows were the other test. A widow without family or money could be left destitute, and James defined pure religion as visiting "orphans and widows in their affliction" (James 1:27). The Jerusalem church ran a daily distribution for its widows, and its first recorded quarrel was over whether some were being overlooked (Acts 6:1). Two centuries later a bishop of Rome, listing his church's staff in a letter, added that it supported "over fifteen hundred widows and persons in distress."

When the persecutions came, the church's heroes included women without rank. Blandina, a slave girl tortured at Lyons in 177, was the one the crowds could not break, though her friends had feared she was too frail to hold out. Perpetua, a young mother in Carthage, kept a prison diary in 203 that is among the earliest surviving Christian writings from a woman's hand. In the fourth century Macrina chose the life of prayer and poverty before any of her famous brothers, and one of them, a bishop and theologian, wrote of her as his teacher.

## How It Was Lost

Then the record turns, and Christians should tell this part themselves. The same centuries that honored Blandina produced Tertullian's sentence. The church that fed fifteen hundred widows went on to teach, in its best schools, that a woman was a lesser kind of man. The room women had been given narrowed. Their names dropped out of the story; the site's essay on [women in church history](/writing/women-in-church-history) tells how many had to be recovered.

The harm was done in the name of the faith by people who held the faith sincerely, and it can't be filed under some other heading. The question is whether they got it from Jesus. On the evidence above they did not. Aquinas took his sentence from Aristotle, and he said so. Contempt for women was in the world before the church was, and the church too often took it in and gave it the standing of doctrine. That is a serious sin, and it ought to trouble Christians more than it does that the pagan Hilarion and the Christian Tertullian could sometimes sound alike.

The history also has a later side that the charge leaves out. A missionary in India campaigned for decades against the burning of widows and lived to see it outlawed in 1829. Pandita Ramabai, an Indian scholar, rescued widows and famine orphans and translated Scripture into Marathi. Christians have no right to set those against the harm and call the account settled. Both are in the record, and the record is mixed because the church has been.

## The Question Christians Still Argue

On one matter faithful Christians read the same passages and come out in different places, and it should be said in each side's own terms.

Complementarians, in the words of the site's Study Bible notes, "hold that God created men and women equal in dignity and worth but with different roles." In marriage the husband leads by giving himself up, as Christ did, and in the church the office of elder is kept for qualified men. Their strongest argument is that Paul grounds what he says in creation and in Christ, and not in Roman custom. They insist that the calling laid on the husband is the heavier one and that it gives no cover to harshness.

Egalitarians "hold that men and women are equal in dignity and in role." They read "submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ" (Ephesians 5:21) as governing everything that follows, and Paul's limit in 1 Timothy as an answer to false teaching in one city. Their strongest argument is the women Paul himself names and praises. They hold that Paul worked inside the household of his day while changing it from within.

The notes call this "a second-order question: it divides faithful churches but not the faith." The site's page on [whether Christianity is bad for women](/questions/morality/is-christianity-bad-for-women) sets the two readings out at more length and says where its author lands, and this essay leaves that there. A longer essay takes up [whether women should preach](/writing/should-women-preach).

What neither side may do is hide behind its position. A church that keeps one office for men has to show by what it does that it holds women equal. Are they taught as seriously, heard as readily, believed as quickly? A church that opens every office to women is not safe from this history either, because abusers have sheltered under both arrangements. Jesus told his disciples how the rulers of the nations lord it over their subjects, and then he said, "It shall not be so among you" (Matthew 20:26).

## If a Church Is Where It Happened

The site's notes on the submission passages say something this essay repeats whole. "Nothing here licenses harshness or abuse. Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice. Abuse and other crimes are to be reported to the police and the proper authorities." And they add: "If you are being hurt in some other place, at home, at work or in a church, the same is true. Tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn."

If the person who hurt you quoted the Bible while he did it, you were not hearing the Bible. You were hearing a man use it. The difference will not undo what happened, and nobody should hurry you past it. [Find Help](/help) lists hotlines you can reach today, and none of them will ask what church you belong to.

## What the Question Comes To

So is Christianity good for women? Christians have often been bad for them, and have used Scripture to do it. Jesus was not. The first churches, where they followed him, were places a slave girl could be remembered by name and a widow would be fed. Where the church has kept his way with women it has been good news for them, and where it borrowed the world's contempt and called it theology it has done great harm. Both have happened, and no slogan covers the record.

The book of Judges contains the worst story in the Bible about what men do to a woman. She is never named and never speaks. The narrator offers no comment and lets the horror stand, and the chapter ends with what was said by all who saw it: "consider it, take counsel, and speak" (Judges 19:30). Scripture didn't hide that story, and the church has no leave to hide its own.

One evening Jesus sat at the table of a religious man named Simon. A woman the town knew as a sinner came in and wept at his feet, and Simon watched and drew his conclusions about them both. Jesus turned toward the woman and spoke to the man. "Do you see this woman?" (Luke 7:44).

Simon had been looking at her the whole time. The church has been asked that question in every century, and the woman in the back row is waiting to hear how it answers.

*"So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them."* (Genesis 1:27)

*"Do you see this woman?"* (Luke 7:44)
